To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
corticospinals excitability is altered during the preparatory phase in humans with chronic cervical spinal cord in incomplete cervical spinal cord injury compared with controls.
corticospinals excitability is altered during movement preparation in patients with incomplete chronic SCI.
corticospinals function is altered in humans with chronic SCI in the preparatory phases of upcoming movements.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of corticospinal pathways in individuals with spinal cord injury (injury at C5–T6 level) and healthy individuals.
the understanding of how the nervous system adapts to spinal cord injury and how these changes may be used for therapeutic intervention.
the study of the corticospinals system, the main motor pathway of the human brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the corticospinals system of humans with SCI is impaired during motor preparation, but the precise mechanisms underlying this impairment remain to be elucidated.
the corticospinals pathway is impaired in SCI, both in the execution of movements and in the preparatory phases of movements.
corticospital excitability is altered during movement preparation in individuals with SCI, and this is probably related to the impairment of transmission at the cortical and spinal levels after SCI.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
SCI leads to a deficit in corticospin transmission in the preparation phase for an upcoming movement.
the ability to alter corticospinal drive in the preparatory period of an upcoming movement is impaired in SCI.
corticospinals transmission is altered in the preparation phase of an upcoming rapid voluntary contraction in humans with chronic SCI.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the corticospinally driven spinal circuitry is impaired in humans with chronic cervical incomplete SCI, even when the task does not require a voluntary movement.
the corticospinals system is altered in individuals with SCI, even when they are not actively performing a movement.
the ability to alter corticospinal output during movement preparation is altered in SCI and that this deficit may be related to impaired transmission of corticospinal input in the spinal cord.
